display_name: Wind Gap Woodruff Vineyard Pinot Noir, Santa Cruz Mountains
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "The Woodruff Vineyard sits at an elevation where morning fog lingers just long enough to preserve brightness, then yields to the intense afternoon light that Santa Cruz Mountains Pinot Noir needs to develop real complexity. Wind Gap's approach here is deliberately restrained—whole cluster fermentation with native yeasts, minimal sulfur, no new oak—so the wine speaks about the site rather than the cellar. This is exactly the kind of bottling that makes Santa Cruz Mountains Pinot Noir worth seeking out.",
  "wine_summary": "Wind Gap has built a reputation for making wines that feel more like geological documents than beverage products. Their Santa Cruz Mountains Pinot Noirs in particular avoid the ripe, high-alcohol trap that many California producers fall into, instead chasing freshness and site transparency. Woodruff Vineyard provides the perfect canvas for this philosophy—thin soils over fractured shale force the vines to work hard, extracting minerals and concentration from relatively young vines. The 2013 vintage earned a silver at TEXSOM, which undersells how compelling this wine actually is.",
  "terroir_expression": "The Santa Cruz Mountains AVA sits above the marine fog layer for much of the day, but Woodruff Vineyard catches enough of that coastal moisture to maintain acidity while still ripening Pinot Noir fully. The fractured shale and sandstone soils drain quickly after winter rains, which stresses the vines without shutting them down. That stress response concentrates flavors and creates the kind of mineral backbone that makes this wine feel more Burgundian than Californian. Iron-rich red soils appear in patches, adding subtle earthiness that shows up as a ferrous note on the finish.",
  "vinification_summary": "Wind Gap's 2013 Woodruff Vineyard Pinot Noir was made with significant whole cluster inclusion—likely in the 30-50% range based on the wine's structure. Whole cluster fermentation adds stem-derived phenolics that provide structure without the hard edges of heavily oaked wines. Native yeast fermentation lets the indigenous microbial terroir of the vineyard express itself, which Wind Gap believes creates more distinctive wines than inoculation. The wine saw used oak, probably neutral French barrels, which adds texture without dominating the fruit. This is a winemaking approach that prioritizes transparency over amenability.",
  "food_pairing": [
    "Pan-seared duck breast with cherry reduction—the wine's earthy undertones and bright acidity cut through the fat while the fruit echoes the cherry sauce",
    "Salted plum and pork belly rice bowls—the wine's mineral edge balances the richness and its light body doesn't overwhelm the dish",
    "Oyster mushrooms with soy butter over soba noodles—a vegetarian option that works because the wine's umami quality meets similar flavors in the mushrooms",
    "Grilled lamb chops with rosemary—this pairing works because the herb notes in the lamb mirror the slight stem character in the wine",
    "Nashville hot chicken sandwich with pickles—the wine's acidity and lack of oak let it cut through the spice and richness of the breading"
  ],
  "comparable_wines": [
    "Sandhi Bent Rock Vineyard Pinot Noir — shares the Santa Cruz Mountains mineral character and restrained winemaking, though Sandhi leans slightly richer",
    "Arnot-Roberts Clary Ranch Pinot Noir — similarly minimal approach with whole cluster, from a Sonoma Coast site that provides comparable tension between fruit and earth",
    "Domaine de la Tournelle Arbois Pupillin Pinot Noir — for those who want to understand the direction Wind Gap is heading, this Jura example shows what whole cluster does in a cooler climate"
  ],
  "style_profile": "Light-to-medium bodied dry red with bright acidity, moderate tannins, and pronounced mineral earthiness",
  "cellar_recommendation": "The 2013 is likely past its peak window for new purchases, but properly stored bottles could still deliver. Look instead for the 2014 or newer releases, which should have more freshness. Store bottles flat in a cool cellar or wine refrigerator, ideally between 50-55°F.",
  "value_assessment": "Wind Gap Pinot Noir from Santa Cruz Mountains typically retails between $35-$50. At this price, it competes with Sonoma Coast producers like Flowers or Williams Selyem, but Woodruff Vineyard offers more mineral complexity than most of those alternatives. The TEXSOM silver on the 2013 was modest recognition for a wine that punches above its weight for terroir transparency.",
  "market_position": "This wine appears on progressive restaurant lists in coastal cities—places that have moved past the Napa Cab paradigm and want something that challenges their guests. Retail distribution is limited and inconsistent, so finding it requires either a dedicated indie wine shop or direct purchase from the winery. The collector audience for Wind Gap skews toward Burgundy-focused drinkers who want to explore California without sacrificing authenticity.",
  "insider_take": "Most people who try Wind Gap expect California fruit-bomb Pinot and are confused by the stemmy, austere character. That's a mistake—they're tasting the winemaking, not a flaw. The real question is whether you want a wine that tastes like wine or a wine that tastes like a place. If the former, move along. If the latter, this delivers something rare in California: genuine site specificity at a price that doesn't require a second mortgage.",
  "aging_potential_years": null,
  "drinking_window_min_years": null,
  "drinking_window_max_years": null,
  "sensory": {
    "acidity": 4,
    "tannin": 3,
    "body": 2,
    "sweetness": 1,
    "alcohol": 3,
    "color_intensity": "pale",
    "aroma_intensity": "pronounced",
    "finish_length": "long",
    "complexity": "complex",
    "quality_level": "very_good"
  }
}
